name: Phyllanthus species (P. amarus, P. urinaria, P. niruri and others)
short: Hepatitis B trials of several Phyllanthus species: no serious adverse events reported, and few or no side effects; but adverse-event reporting was sparse, and species and preparations varied.
text: These data pool several Phyllanthus species tested in chronic hepatitis B infection, including people described as hepatitis B carriers. The abstracts rarely state the form, though one trial used capsules. Amla (Phyllanthus emblica) has its own entry. A 2011 Cochrane review of 16 randomised trials (1,326 patients) of Phyllanthus species, alone or added to antiviral drugs, found that only two trials reported adverse-event numbers, without significant differences, and that no serious adverse events were reported; a 2013 Cochrane review of five trials comparing compound phyllanthus, a preparation its abstract does not describe further, with antiviral drugs found no adverse-event data at all, and a 2001 systematic review of 22 trials reported no serious adverse event. By species: in a 12-month placebo-controlled trial of Phyllanthus niruri in 50 people with chronic hepatitis B, kidney-function tests did not change and no serious adverse events occurred due to the treatment; in a 6-month placebo-controlled trial of Phyllanthus urinaria (spelled urinaris in the abstract) no serious adverse event was reported. In trials of Phyllanthus amarus in hepatitis B carriers, the authors of a 65-person placebo-controlled trial using capsules write that adverse effects ‘were not observed in all patients receiving the plant’, a phrase that does not make clear whether any patient had one, and give no adverse-event numbers; in 30 carriers it was well tolerated, with no clinical side effects or changes in the organ profiles used for safety evaluation; and a 1988 study saw few or no toxic effects. The reviews note that trial quality was generally low and that species and preparations varied. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
